In [[mathematical statistics]], the '''Ghosh-Pratt identity''' is a theorem that establishes a formal relationship between the expected volume of a [[confidence set]] and its probability of false coverage. It is a cornerstone of [[optimal estimation]], as it allows the problem of finding the shortest [[confidence interval]] to be framed as a problem of maximizing the power of a [[statistical test]].

The identity was independently discovered and published in 1961 by the Indian statistician [[Jayanta Kumar Ghosh]] and the American statistician [[John Winsor Pratt]].

==Formal statement==
Let <math>X</math> be a [[random variable]] with a [[probability distribution]] indexed by a parameter <math>\theta \in \Theta</math>. Let <math>C(X)</math> denote a random variable representing a confidence set for <math>\theta</math>. The Ghosh-Pratt identity states that the expected volume (or length, if <math>\Theta</math> is one dimensional) of the confidence set <math>C(X)</math>, calculated under the true parameter value <math>\theta_0</math>, is equal to the integral of the probabilities of including false values of <math>\theta</math> in the set:
:<math>\operatorname{E}_{\theta_0} [ \text{vol}(C(X))] = \int_{\theta \neq \theta_0} P_{\theta_0} (\theta \in C(X)) \, d\theta</math>
In simpler terms, the expected length of a confidence interval is the sum (integral) of the probabilities of covering all possible incorrect values of <math>\theta</math>.<ref name="Pratt1961">{{cite journal |last1=Pratt |first1=John W. |year=1961 |title=Length of Confidence Intervals |journal=[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]] |volume=56 |issue=295 |pages=549–567 |doi=10.1080/01621459.1961.10480644 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1961.10480644|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Derivation==
The proof of the identity relies on the relationship between the volume of a set and the [[indicator function]]. Given a specific realization of data <math>x</math>, let <math>C(x)</math> be an arbitrary confidence set for the parameter <math>\theta</math>. The volume of this set, <math>\text{vol}(C(x))</math>, can be expressed as:
:<math>\text{vol}(C(x)) = \int_{\Theta} I(\theta \in C(x)) \, d\theta</math>
where <math>I(\cdot)</math> is the indicator function. To find the expected volume under the true parameter <math>\theta_0</math>, we consider all possible confidence sets across the data generating process <math>X</math> and take the [[expected value]] with respect to the distribution of <math>X</math> given <math>\theta_0</math>:
:<math>\text{E}_{\theta_0} [\text{vol}(C(X))] = \text{E}_{\theta_0} \left[ \int_{\Theta} I(\theta \in C(X)) \, d\theta \right]</math>

By applying [[Fubini's theorem]], we can reverse the order of expectation:
:<math>\text{E}_{\theta_0} [\text{vol}(C(X))] = \int_{\Theta} \text{E}_{\theta_0} [I(\theta \in C(X))] \, d\theta</math>

Since the expectation of an indicator function is simply the probability of the event indicated:
:<math>\text{E}_{\theta_0} [I(\theta \in C(X))] = \text{P}_{\theta_0}(\theta \in C(X))</math>

Substituting this false coverage probability back into the integral yields the identity:
:<math>E_{\theta_0} [\text{vol}(C(X))] = \int_{\Theta} P_{\theta_0}(\theta \in C(X)) \, d\theta</math>
This result shows that the expected volume is the integral of the probability that the confidence set covers any value <math>\theta</math> (both the true value <math>\theta_0</math> as well as all false values <math>\theta \neq \theta_0</math>).

==Generalization==
While the identity is often presented in the context of a [[continuous random variable]], it can be generalized using [[measure theory]] to cover [[discrete random variable]]s and mixed distributions as well. If <math>\mu</math> is a [[sigma-finite measure]] on the parameter space <math>\Theta</math>, the expected measure of the confidence set <math>C(X)</math> under the distribution <math>P_{\theta_0}</math> is given by:
:<math>\text{E}_{\theta_0} [\mu(C(X))] = \int_{\Theta} P_{\theta_0}(\theta \in C(X)) \, \mu(d\theta)</math>
This general form demonstrates that the identity is independent of the underlying distribution of the data <math>X</math>: whether it is a [[continuous random variable]] or a [[discrete random variable]], the relationship between the expected size of the set and the probability of coverage still holds. In other words, the choice of the measure <math>\mu</math> is application-specific:
* If <math>\mu</math> is the [[Lebesgue measure]], we obtain the standard formula for the expected volume of an interval in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>.
* If <math>\mu</math> is the [[counting measure]], we obtain the formula for the expected number of points in a discrete set.

This mathematical framework ensures the identity is a robust tool across diverse statistical models.<ref name="Cornell" />

==Significance and applications==
The identity is significant because it connects [[estimation theory]] with [[hypothesis testing]]. Since a confidence set is often constructed by inverting a family of hypothesis tests, the identity shows that:
* to minimize the expected length of a confidence interval, one must minimize the probability of covering false values, and
* minimizing the probability of covering false values is equivalent to maximizing the [[statistical power]] of the underlying hypothesis test.

By applying the [[Neyman-Pearson lemma]], which identifies [[uniformly most powerful test]]s, statisticians can use the Ghosh-Pratt identity to construct confidence intervals that are mathematically guaranteed to be the shortest possible on average.<ref name="Ghosh1961">{{cite journal |last1=Ghosh |first1=J. K. |year=1961 |title=On the relation among shortest confidence intervals of different types |journal=Calcutta Statistical Association Bulletin |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=147–152 |doi=10.1177/0008068319610404 |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/0008068319610404|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==History==
The identity was published nearly simultaneously in 1961. J.K. Ghosh published his findings in the ''[[Calcutta Statistical Association Bulletin]]'', focusing on the relationship between interval types, while John Pratt published his in the ''[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]]'' focusing on the [[decision theory|decision-theoretic]] implications. While the two approached the problem from slightly different perspectives, their results were mathematically equivalent.<ref name="Cornell">{{cite web |last1=Casella |first1=George |author-link=George Casella|title=The Ghosh-Pratt Identity |url=https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/1813/31908/1/BU-1314-M.pdf |publisher=Cornell University eCommons |year=1996 |access-date=2026-01-31}}</ref>
